title: Less me
hook: setting the self aside to make room for the divine

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah b'gashmiyut, service through the body. Your line was serve through the body. Did one meal today begin with a pause? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

Abraham is arguing with God. Two cities are about to be destroyed, and Abraham, with nothing to bargain with, keeps pressing. What if there are fifty good people there? Forty-five? Forty? He's bold. He's bargaining with the Judge of all the earth. And right in the middle of that boldness, he stops and says something about himself. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, he calls himself one "who am but dust and ashes." Bold and small in the same breath. The Hasidic teachers built a whole practice on that combination, and today's word names it.
screen: `ABRAHAM ARGUES WITH GOD.` → `BOLD.` → `AND DUST AND ASHES.`

segments.voice: Bittul. Setting aside, making void, the self stepping out of the way. In Hasidic teaching, bittul is the practice of making less of yourself so there is room for God. First, the two models. Abraham says he is dust and ashes. Moses, too, is remembered this way: the Torah says, "Now the man Moses was very meek." And when the people complain, Moses and Aaron answer, in effect, what are we? The Talmud sets those sayings side by side, as if each is a step further into getting out of the way. Second, it is not self-hatred. Abraham doesn't stop arguing because he's dust. He argues harder. Moses is meek and leads a nation. Bittul isn't thinking you're worthless. It's not making yourself the center. Third, the vessel. Hasidic teachers use the picture of a container. A cup already full to the brim has no space for what's being poured. Pour out a little of the self, and there's room. That's why yesterday's teaching and this one fit together: the body can serve, and the self can step aside so the service is for God and not for show. Fourth, the everyday version. Bittul can be as small as letting someone else's idea win in a meeting when theirs is better. Not mentioning your part in a success. Listening to the end of a sentence without preparing your reply. Small acts of less me, so that something larger has room.
screen: `DUST AND ASHES. WHAT ARE WE?` · `NOT SELF-HATRED.` · `A CUP FULL OF ITSELF CAN'T RECEIVE.` · `SMALL ACTS OF STEPPING ASIDE.` · then, large: `LESS ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make yourself smaller once. Settle, and breathe. Notice how much of the inside of your head is about you: what you need to say, how you're coming across, what you're owed. Don't fight it. Just notice its size. Now, for a few breaths, set it down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag. Let the room, the sounds, the people you love, take up the space instead. If you pray, you can stand before God as Abraham did, bold and small at once. The bell holds the time.
Bittul. Setting the self aside to make room for the divine. Not self-hatred: an emptier cup, with room to receive. Today's word.
Your line: less me. Today, once, let someone else's idea win, or let a compliment go to someone else, without saying a word about your part. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Hasidic teaching treats bittul as a lifelong practice of humility before God, cultivated in prayer and in ordinary dealings with others, and sees it as the ground of a person's service.

fork.setup: you're Abraham. you've just called yourself dust and ashes before God. what do you do next?
options: fall silent, since dust has no right to speak.
keep pressing: what if there are fewer good people?
fork.reveal: he keeps bargaining, fifty, forty-five, forty and on. his smallness doesn't silence him. it makes room for the plea.

original.note: Hebrew: setting aside, making void. In Hasidism, the self stepping out of the way.

what it means: setting the self aside so there is room for God, while still acting, speaking and arguing.
what a scholar hears: a Hasidic ideal modeled on Abraham's 'dust and ashes' and Moses' meekness, set side by side in the Talmud's reading.
